idiom_name: ThreadLocal<RequestContext> bound by a servlet filter / Spring request scope
implementation_notes: On servlet containers the structure becomes a container-managed request scope: a filter or front controller writes the context into a ThreadLocal (or a @RequestScope bean), the rest of the stack reads it through a static accessor. It is the pragmatic default and needs no signature changes, but ThreadLocal has unbounded lifetime and unconstrained mutability - bind in a try and call remove() in finally, or the value leaks into the next request on that pooled thread.
pitfalls: A ThreadLocal that is not removed in a finally block keeps the value (and the request's classloader) alive for the next request handled by that thread.
ThreadLocal does not follow work handed to an executor or a virtual thread unless the value is captured explicitly, so async branches see stale or missing context.

variants.name: Explicit Context class threaded through the layers (Core J2EE form)
variants.idiom_name: ServiceContext + ServiceContextFactory passed as a parameter
variants.implementation_notes: The original Core J2EE form: a Context class with typed accessors, a ContextFactory that creates and populates it from the request, and layer methods that take the context as an argument - no ambient state, so lifetime and testability are fully explicit. Choose it when layers must stay framework-independent, when several parallel contexts coexist in one request, or when you want the dependency visible in signatures; the cost is one extra parameter on every method between producer and consumer.
pitfalls: Every intermediate method must repeat the parameter, which is exactly the signature noise the pattern is meant to absorb - if the chain is deep, only the layers that need the context should carry it.
A context shared by reference is mutable; either make it immutable or define precisely which layer may write which field, otherwise concurrent layers race on the same instance.

variants.name: ScopedValue immutable bindings (JDK 25)
variants.implementation_notes: ScopedValue (final in JDK 25, JEP 506) is the JDK's answer to the ambient form: a static final ScopedValue is bound for the dynamic scope of one where(...).run()/call() invocation, read with get(), and inherited by child threads created in a StructuredTaskScope without the copying cost of thread-locals. It removes the two classic ThreadLocal failure modes - a binding cannot be mutated by far-away code and its lifetime is bounded by the enclosing lambda - at the price of write-once immutability and no ability for callees to enrich the context for their own callees.
pitfalls: A binding is visible only inside the lambda passed to run/call; code that escapes that scope (queued tasks, registered callbacks) throws instead of reading a stale value - a behaviour change for code migrating from ThreadLocal.
There is no setter by design: a callee cannot rebind the value it sees for its own callees except by nesting another where(...).run(...).
